scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): grants that breadth helps, then argues it is not the single best way to educate; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: Universities often debate how to turn students into genuinely educated people.
Some people argue that requiring students to take courses outside their major is the best way to ensure they become truly educated.
I agree that such breadth helps, but I do not believe it is the single best way to educate a student.
First, studying outside one's major genuinely broadens a student's mind.
Learning across several fields helps students connect ideas and see the world more fully.
For example, a science student who studies ethics may think more wisely about how her work affects people.
This shows that variety can make a student more thoughtful and well-rounded.
Such breadth builds flexible skills, like reasoning and writing, that are useful in any career.
Students also discover unexpected interests through subjects they would never have chosen alone.
To this extent, requiring some breadth clearly helps students grow.

sections.role: Body 2 — Why it is not the best way

sentences.text: Second, however, calling breadth the best way to ensure a true education claims too much.
Real education depends just as much on the depth and quality of what is taught.
Consider a student who takes many varied courses but learns each one only shallowly.
Such a scattered education can leave a student knowing a little about much and a lot about nothing.
Great teaching, curiosity, and the habit of questioning matter at least as much as variety.
A deep mastery of one field can also make a person truly educated in important ways.
Breadth, then, is one valuable path to education but certainly not the only or best one.
In conclusion, studying outside one's major does help make students well-rounded.
But it is only one part of a true education, not the single best way to achieve it.
Students become truly educated through depth, good teaching, and curiosity as much as through breadth.
